I am 73 years old and have worked this land for 50 years. With only my wife and me at home, I must choose crops that I can manage with my own two hands, even though they are not as strong as before. My 4.1 mu is small, but I know every inch of it. I have grown cotton intercropped with mungbean for many years, and this system still works for me. In early April, when the soil warms, I rotary-till the 3 mu field and sow cotton and mungbean together—mungbean goes between the cotton rows. I use improved seeds, the kinds sold at the county supply store that I have used before and trust. Before sowing, I spread 100 kg of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu, which gives me 15 kg of nitrogen, 15 kg of phosphorus, and 15 kg of potassium per mu. Cotton is hungry for nutrients and water, so I irrigate twice from my well: once at flowering and once during boll formation. I also spray pesticides about 14 times through the season. I know that is a lot of work, but cotton pests—especially bollworm—will ruin the crop if I get lazy. The mungbean shares the same field, so it gets the same fertilizer, water, and pest sprays. I harvest the mungbean in summer when the pods are ripe, and I expect about 100 kg per mu. The cotton stays in the field until autumn, and I usually get around 550 kg of seed cotton per mu. For millet, I plant about 1 mu in summer. Millet is good food for our household and does not need much attention. I put down about 80 kg of compound fertilizer per mu, giving roughly 12 kg each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium per mu, and irrigate once if the rains are poor. Maybe two pesticide sprays if insects show up. Millet is tough and usually gives me about 700 kg per mu. This is my plan. It is what I have always done, and at my age, I see no reason to change what works.
